title: Entropic Frameworks of Human Motricity, Athletic Anti-Entropy, and Neuromuscular Aging: A Scientific Review
content: Human motricity operates within a continuous balance between biological organization and disorder. This focused scientific review synthesizes evidence linking movement entropy, lifespan neuromuscular decline, motor-unit remodeling, rapid force production, denervation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and high-velocity training. Longitudinal cohorts show that physical capacity and muscle power peak in early adulthood and decline progressively thereafter. Motor-unit number estimates indicate substantial loss with aging, while surviving units enlarge through collateral reinnervation. Meta-analytic evidence also shows lower motor-unit discharge rates and modestly reduced voluntary activation in older adults. Mechanistic human data identify the first 50 ms of explosive force production as especially dependent on neural excitation; in active octogenarians, normalized 0-50 ms RFD is selectively impaired. Disuse can alter motor-unit properties and neuromuscular-junction transmission within 21 days, while persistent sporadic denervation in very old muscle is linked mechanistically to mitochondrial dysfunction. Histological muscle entropy is independently associated with lower power, mobility, and mitochondrial energetics. Together, these findings support an integrative neuromuscular-aging framework in which neural, motor-unit, tissue, and bioenergetic changes interact across the lifespan. High-velocity power training is presented as a targeted countermeasure for preserving rapid force and function, while several causal links remain to be tested longitudinally.
